summary: Weekly POC check-in focused on improving Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) and streaming performance. Reviewed current bench results (p50/p95), discussed kernel choices (triton/flash attention vs cuBLAS), sequence length tradeoffs and KV-cache behavior. Agreed next steps to run a 1k concurrent streaming benchmark, share logs and kernel configs, and schedule a kernel tuning deep dive.
topics: Streaming vs non-streaming first byte behavior
Kernel selection: Triton / FlashAttention / cuBLAS fallbacks
KV cache and prefix caching impact
Dedicated vs Hosted and burst capacity tradeoffs
Security docs (SOC2, KMS) and VPC peering
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: hey everyone, thanks for joining. were on for 45 minutes today, quick sync on the latency POC. Samir youll lead the perf bits, Aisha and team can walk through what you saw last week.
[00:12] Aisha Gomez: thanks, Jordan. yea we ran the baseline tests, streaming enabled, using the r-llm-13b variant you provisioned. p50 is around 48ms for first byte but p95 spikes to ~340ms on longer prompts.
[00:28] Samir Patel: ok that's useful. couple clarifications: those numbers are from the hosted pool or Dedicated nodes?
[00:35] Aisha Gomez: hosted. we haven't switched to dedicated yet. we did a small dedicated run but it was noisy.
[00:42] Jordan Lee: got it. our expectation for streaming-first-byte with that model and the default kernel is p50 < 60ms, p95 sub-200ms on 512 token typical sequences. 340ms is high, so suspect either kernel falling back or batching spikes.
[00:58] Tom Reeves: also noticed CPU on the edge box spikes during the streaming tests, maybe TLS termination or our side.
[01:05] Samir Patel: yeah possible. couple things we'll confirm: 1) whether Triton fused kernels were used or cuBLAS fallback, 2) whether KV cache is warmed, 3) batch window/continuous-batching settings.
[01:18] Mei Chen: quick dumb question: what's KV cache warming look like for streaming? does it help first-byte?
[01:23] Samir Patel: good question. KV cache helps subsequent tokens and reduces compute for long conversations, but first-byte is mostly kernel startup + tokenization + initial attention key building. streaming first byte can be improved by pre-allocating and keeping model in hot use or using our fast-start path.
[01:35] Aisha Gomez: when you say fast-start path is that the Dedicated warm pool? or is that something handled in the hosted control plane?
[01:42] Jordan Lee: both. we have a fast-start runtime that reduces kernel launch and memory init for hot containers; Dedicated gives more control to keep GPUs pinned and reduces cold-start variance.
[01:50] Carlos Diaz: we saw variance when sequence lengths exceed 1024. At 2048 p95 jumps a lot. We primarily operate on 512 median, but we have a tail of longer queries.
[02:02] Samir Patel: that makes sense. attention kernel characteristics change with seq length; some kernels (FlashAttention/triton) are much faster for mid-range sequences, but for very long sequences the memory layout causes additional copies or fallback to cuBLAS.
[02:16] Aisha Gomez: is there a recommended kernel config for 512 vs 2048? we tried default and 'auto' but it still fell back sometimes.
[02:23] Samir Patel: for 512 we typically enable Triton fused kernels + 8-bit quantization profile if QA accepts minor quality delta. For 2048, we often switch to FlashAttention or our tiled attention kernels. but there's tradeoffs. also check whether your tokenizer batching is adding prefixes.
[02:37] Mei Chen: QA team is sensitive to hallucination changes from quantization. we'd rather not degrade quality in prod.
[02:43] Jordan Lee: understood. we can run a quantization A/B on a small eval set from your prompts to measure delta. thats a next step.
[02:51] Tom Reeves: about TTFT specifically, we measured cold-container first byte at ~220ms and hot-container at ~45ms. what counts as cold here? container restart or kernel fallback?
[03:01] Samir Patel: cold often is container or model reload. kernel fallback due to sequence shape mismatch can also add 50-150ms. We have telemetry to show kernel path per request; I'll pull that.
[03:12] Jordan Lee: Samir can share the kernel-path logs. Samir?
[03:15] Samir Patel: yea I'll run another bench with tracing on. plan: streaming enabled, seq=512 primary, 1k concurrent simulated users at 10rps each for 60s, capture kernel-paths and TTFT percentiles.
[03:28] Aisha Gomez: thatd be great. also can you include the tokenization time split? we saw ~12ms tokenization which is non-trivial.
[03:36] Samir Patel: yep we'll include tokenization and network hop times.
[03:40] Carlos Diaz: on our infra side, we can open a peering window next Friday to test from our VPC. we'll send firewall rules.
[03:47] Jordan Lee: nice. Elena will send the SOC2 docs and KMS notes to unblock VPC peering.
[03:53] Elena Ruiz: will do, short note with links after call.
[03:56] Mei Chen: back to kernel choices, how risky is switching to Triton fused kernels? any stability or repro issues?
[04:03] Samir Patel: Triton fused is mature but dependent on sequence shapes. if shape variance is high we can use shape clustering to group requests or fallback to tiled kernels. we also offer a hybrid config that prefers fused but falls back with a sub-50ms penalty typically.
[04:18] Aisha Gomez: can we pin that hybrid config for Dedicated during POC? we want stability first.
[04:23] Jordan Lee: yes you can pin. Dedicated also gives more deterministic perf. There's a cost delta but we can show unit economics for your traffic pattern.
[04:31] Tom Reeves: what about batching? we saw micro-bursts that introduced 40-60ms extra latency.
[04:36] Samir Patel: micro-bursts often from our batch window. we can reduce max batch window to lower latency at cost of throughput. Continuous batching strategies can also help. We'll test with a 5ms vs 20ms batching window.
[04:47] Aisha Gomez: could you summarize what you will test and what we need to give you?
[04:51] Samir Patel: sure: tests: 1) streaming 1k users seq=512 with triton preferred, record kernel path & TTFT; 2) same with hybrid kernels and reduced batch window; 3) dedicated small node run to show pinned GPU variance. We need: prompt corpus (~200), expected p95 targets, VPC peering window.
[05:05] Jordan Lee: and we'll also run a quant A/B on 100 prompts to measure quality delta if you authorize.
[05:11] Aisha Gomez: yes authorize A/B for non-prod flagged prompts, QA will review.
[05:15] Carlos Diaz: I'll slot a peering window next Friday 09:00-11:00 our side.
[05:21] Samir Patel: perfect. I'll start the bench and share a link to raw logs + a small dashboard.
[05:26] Tom Reeves: also just flagging encryption at rest, we want KMS integration. how tight is that with Dedicated?
[05:31] Jordan Lee: Dedicated supports customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM; Elena will share the integration notes.
[05:36] Mei Chen: any blockers we should be aware of for the streaming test?
[05:39] Samir Patel: only blocker is VPC peering and firewall for the dedicated run; for hosted runs we just need the prompt set. If you want end-to-end realistic latencies we need to test from your VPC.
[05:50] Aisha Gomez: ok we'll prioritize peering.
[05:52] Jordan Lee: ok quick recap: Samir runs benchmark and shares logs by 7/9, Jordan shares Dedicated pricing by 7/8, Aisha sends prompts and p95 target by 7/8, Elena sends SOC2/KMS links by 7/7, Carlos sends peering details by 7/9. any other items?
[06:08] Aisha Gomez: one last ask: can you include the kernel selection heuristics in the doc? e.g. when do you pick triton vs flash vs cuBLAS?
[06:16] Samir Patel: yep I'll include a short doc explaining heuristics and the config flags.
[06:20] Jordan Lee: great. thanks everyone, see you next week same time.
[06:24] (call ends)
